Dr. Reed: Right, come in. So for your research project you want to study New Year resolutions — talk me through it.
Anna: We're comparing two groups: people who wrote resolutions down versus people who only said them out loud. We'll follow both for six weeks into February.
Dr. Reed: A classic design — self-report versus written commitment. How many participants do you need?
Mo: We were thinking twenty per group, but with dropouts we'd better recruit fifty in total — twenty-five per group.
Dr. Reed: Sensible. Recruiting them?
Anna: A notice on the campus board and two WeChat groups for postgraduates. We've already got nine sign-ups from the campus group alone.
Dr. Reed: You'll need informed consent forms — remember ethics approval before you collect a single name. And make sure the survey is anonymous; don't record names next to the answers.
Mo: Got it. We'll store the data in an encrypted file on the university drive, and destroy it after the submission deadline.
Dr. Reed: Good. What are you actually measuring? How do you define “success”?
Anna: We're not asking “did you succeed” directly — instead, weekly check-ins: “How many days this week did you act on your resolution?” Zero to seven. Then we compare the two groups.
Dr. Reed: And the analysis?
Mo: Descriptive stats for the progress charts, and a simple t-test to compare the two groups' mean scores at week six.
Dr. Reed: Fine for an undergraduate project. One caution — self-report bias. People will say they did better than they did. Consider asking a friend or family member to verify one behaviour, like going to the gym.
Anna: That's a good point. We could add a “behaviour check” question at week three and week six: “Did someone else witness this habit?”
Dr. Reed: Exactly. And the timeline — when is the write-up due?
Mo: The 20th of March. Interviews done by mid-February, analysis March 1st to 10th, draft by the 15th, final version the 20th.
Dr. Reed: Tight but doable. One last thing — if someone's resolution involves mental health, don't try to advise them. Refer them to the university counselling service.
Anna & Mo: Of course.
Dr. Reed: Then good luck — and don't make resolution number one be “don't change the research question halfway through”!
